airport: large airport facilities with broad paved aviation areas and terminal-like structures, distinguishing airport from farmland by lacking cultivated parcel texture, from port by lacking shoreline docks and harbor-water context, and from viaduct by lacking a narrow elevated transport crossing.
bareland: broad exposed ground with barren surface and little vegetation, distinguishing bareland from desert by showing less homogeneous arid texture, from mountain by weaker terrain relief, and from forest by lacking dense tree canopy.
baseballfield: compact sports field with a clear baseball-diamond layout and central infield geometry, distinguishing baseballfield from playground by stronger baseball-field structure, from stadium by weaker venue enclosure, and from park by more explicit sports-field markings.
beach: bright shoreline region with clear sand-water boundary and coastal texture, distinguishing beach from port by lacking dock-side transport organization, from river by broader coastal shoreline scale, and from resort by weaker leisure-oriented built structure.
bridge: narrow man-made crossing structure spanning water or land, distinguishing bridge from viaduct by a more localized crossing form, from port by lacking harbor-side logistics infrastructure, and from pond by being a crossing rather than a compact water body.
center: dense urban core with concentrated buildings and organized city-block layout, distinguishing center from stadium by lacking a dominant sports field, from church by weaker single-landmark emphasis, and from commercial by emphasizing a broader civic core rather than a business district.
church: prominent religious building or complex with distinctive landmark-like architecture, distinguishing church from commercial by weaker business-block organization, from square by stronger building dominance, and from center by emphasizing a landmark structure rather than a broad urban core.
commercial: organized business district with dense building blocks and road access, distinguishing commercial from church by lacking landmark-like religious structure, from industrial by lacking heavy factory compounds and storage yards, and from center by stronger business-district texture rather than a civic-core composition.
denseresidential: tightly packed residential roofs with very high housing density and minimal spacing, distinguishing denseresidential from sparseresidential by far denser roof clusters, from mediumresidential by much closer building intervals, and from square by stronger repeated housing-roof structure rather than an open civic space.
desert: wide dry barren region with homogeneous arid texture and very little vegetation, distinguishing desert from bareland by stronger sand-like continuity, from storagetanks by lacking circular industrial structures, and from river by lacking a continuous water channel.
farmland: regular cultivated land with visible parcel boundaries and agricultural texture, distinguishing farmland from meadow by stronger man-made plot organization, from airport by lacking broad paved aviation surfaces, and from river by lacking a continuous watercourse.
forest: dense continuous tree canopy with dark green natural texture, distinguishing forest from pond by lacking a compact water body, from bareland by much stronger vegetation coverage, and from mountain by weaker terrain relief and more canopy-dominant appearance.
industrial: large factory-like compounds with utilitarian structures, storage yards, and production-oriented layouts, distinguishing industrial from storagetanks by not being dominated only by circular tanks, from commercial by weaker business-block texture and stronger yard structure, and from railwaystation by weaker rail-line concentration.
meadow: broad natural grass-covered open area with soft vegetation texture and weak structural boundaries, distinguishing meadow from farmland by lacking regular cultivated parcel boundaries, from pond by being vegetation-dominant rather than water-dominant, and from baseballfield by lacking formal sports-field geometry.
mediumresidential: moderately spaced residential buildings with visible yards and balanced housing density, distinguishing mediumresidential from sparseresidential by denser neighborhood grouping, from denseresidential by larger spacing between houses, and from resort by more regular residential neighborhood structure.
mountain: rugged elevated terrain with strong relief, slope shadows, and irregular topographic texture, distinguishing mountain from bareland by stronger terrain variation, from forest by more obvious relief, and from desert by less homogeneous barren texture.
park: planned green open space with vegetation and leisure-oriented layout, distinguishing park from pond by being land-dominant rather than water-dominant, from square by stronger vegetation presence, and from resort by weaker accommodation-like built structure.
parking: large open paved area with organized parking rows and vehicle-oriented layout, distinguishing parking from industrial by lacking factory-compound structure, from denseresidential by lacking dense roof clusters, and from church by lacking landmark-building dominance.
playground: recreational activity area with sports or play surfaces and open activity layout, distinguishing playground from stadium by weaker venue enclosure, from baseballfield by lacking a baseball-diamond infield, and from park by showing more explicit play-ground geometry.
pond: small enclosed water body with compact shape and visible boundary, distinguishing pond from park by being water-dominant, from forest by lacking continuous canopy, and from river by lacking a long winding channel.
port: waterfront transport area with docks, vessels, and harbor-side logistics infrastructure, distinguishing port from beach by stronger transport and dock organization, from airport by shoreline-water context instead of aviation pavement, and from bridge by lacking a simple crossing structure.
railwaystation: transport hub with concentrated rail lines and station-related structures, distinguishing railwaystation from industrial by clearer rail-line concentration, from commercial by stronger transport-node organization, and from airport by lacking broad aviation runways.
resort: leisure-oriented built environment with organized open spaces and accommodation-like structures, distinguishing resort from port by weaker dock-industrial structure, from park by stronger built tourism layout, and from beach by more visible leisure-oriented built organization beyond the shoreline.
river: elongated natural watercourse with continuous winding channel and visible banks, distinguishing river from beach by narrower inland channel structure, from farmland by lacking regular cultivated parcel boundaries, and from pond by stronger linear flow shape.
school: campus-like area with multiple institutional buildings, open grounds, and organized educational layout, distinguishing school from square by stronger campus structure, from church by weaker landmark-building dominance, and from commercial by less business-district organization.
sparseresidential: widely separated residential houses with large open gaps and low housing density, distinguishing sparseresidential from mediumresidential by larger spacing and lower roof density, from denseresidential by far lower housing density, and from pond by lacking water-dominant appearance.
square: open civic plaza-like space embedded in urban area, distinguishing square from church by weaker landmark-building dominance, from park by less vegetation, and from school by weaker campus-like building organization.
stadium: large sports complex with prominent field and stronger enclosure or spectator-related structure, distinguishing stadium from playground by more venue-like framing, from center by emphasizing a dedicated sports facility, and from baseballfield by larger scale and more stadium-like organization.
storagetanks: clusters of large circular industrial tanks with highly regular round geometry, distinguishing storagetanks from industrial by stronger circular-container dominance, from bareland by lacking barren natural texture, and from desert by lacking broad homogeneous arid surface.
viaduct: elongated elevated transport structure with clear grade-separated linear form, distinguishing viaduct from bridge by a more extended raised-traffic pattern, from airport by lacking broad aviation pavement, and from railwaystation by lacking concentrated station-like rail organization.
